Meet Your Instructor
The
Author
Stephen

Filmmaker · Creator · Educator
For the past 11 years, I've been immersed in the world of visual storytelling.

I started as a photographer and videographer, working on creative projects with individuals, brands, and entrepreneurs — learning how cameras work, how lighting shapes a scene, and how strong visuals can communicate an idea before a single word is spoken.

Over time, what started as a creative pursuit turned into a professional skillset that allowed me to collaborate with brands and grow an audience of over 40,000 followers.

Inside this book, I'll walk you through the Shooting Stars Content Framework — a practical system for creating high-quality content that stands out online.

Whether you're an entrepreneur, business owner, or someone who simply wants better content, this guide gives you the tools and structure to do it.

Let's get started.

P.07 — CAPTURING ATTENTION / BUILDING TRUST
S.1  —  S.2
Shooting Stars: Content FrameworkCh. 01
The Impact Of Strong Content
Attention,
Then Trust
S.1
Capturing
Attention
Every day, millions of pieces of content are posted online. The biggest challenge isn't creating content — it's earning attention. High-quality visuals, clear messaging, and intentional storytelling make people pause when they're scrolling.
The goal isn't to post more. It's to create content people actually stop to watch.
S.2
Building
Trust
When your content looks polished, clear, and well thought out, it signals professionalism. People naturally associate quality with credibility. For creators this builds authority; for businesses it makes customers more confident.
Real effort communicates that you take your message, and your audience, seriously.
Hot Take
Carousel posts build trust seamlessly at this stage — they give people a reason to slow down and read rather than scroll past.

Part 1  /  The Fun Stuff
Do You Know
Your Tools?
Whether you’re filming on a phone, handheld, or a professional camera, the goal is the same: control how your content looks instead of leaving it up to chance.
The difference between average content and high-quality content often comes down to a few key fundamentals: how your image is exposed (lighting), how motion looks (cinematic vs. authentic phone video), and how your subject is framed.
Once you understand these settings, creating strong, premium content becomes much easier and far more consistent.

P.17 — T.2 WHY ISO MATTERS · brightness + noise scale
T.2  —  ISO
Shooting Stars: Content FrameworkCh. 03
T.2  /  Why ISO Matters
Brightness
Has A Price
Higher ISO → brighter image
Lower ISO → darker image
Sensitivity to light
How To Use It
Start with the lowest ISO for your environment.
→
Bright environments keep ISO low
→
Indoor or low light increase ISO gradually
If your image is too dark, you can raise ISO. But first consider opening your aperture or slowing your shutter speed to maintain better image quality.

P.18 — T.3 SHUTTER SPEED = MOTION CONTROL · motion blur diagram
T.3  —  Shutter Speed
Shooting Stars: Content FrameworkCh. 03
T.3  /  Shutter Speed Is Motion Control
Motion, Not
Brightness.
Shutter speed controls motion and motion blur in your footage, determining how long your camera’s sensor is exposed to light for each frame.
Faster shutter
Less motion blur. Sharper, more rigid movement.
Slower shutter
More motion blur. Smoother, more natural movement.
!
Do Not Use It For Exposure
Changing shutter speed does affect exposure, but it should primarily be used to control motion, not lighting. Incorrect shutter speed is one of the fastest ways to make your content look unprofessional, even if everything else is set correctly.

P.20 — T.5 APERTURE · iris + depth of field comparison
T.5  —  Aperture
Shooting Stars: Content FrameworkCh. 03
T.5  /  Create Depth In Your Content
Controlling
Focus & Blur
Aperture controls depth of field: how much of your image is in focus. It also affects how much light enters your lens, which impacts overall exposure.
Lower f-stop
f/1.8 or f/2.8 creates a blurred background and a sharp subject.
Higher f-stop
f/5 or f/8 keeps more of the frame in focus.
The wider the opening, the more light reaches the sensor and the thinner the plane of focus becomes. Depth and exposure move together, which is why aperture is the setting to reach for first.

P.22 — MORE TO BE MINDFUL OF · full-bleed statement
More To Be Mindful Of
Shooting Stars: Content FrameworkCh. 03
More To Be Mindful Of
Shallow depth
cuts both
ways.
Avoid shooting wide open without checking focus. When aperture is low your depth of field is shallow, meaning if you move slightly out of position, you can easily fall out of focus.
Advice From S. Michael
f/2.8 or lower
Talking head videos, or showing a product.
f/4.5 – f/6
B-roll showing a wider frame or an entire environment, so everything stays in focus.
Go Low For
Talking-to-camera content
Product shots
Interviews
Personal brand videos
Go Higher For
Group shots and landscapes. Increase to f/5 or higher when you need more of the scene in focus, and stay mindful, because this affects your lighting.
22
